desc:
For each window of k consecutive elements of nums, report its lower median: sort the window and take the element at (0-based) position (k - 1) / 2, rounded down. For odd k this is the usual median; for even k it is the smaller of the two middle values.

Return the medians of all windows from left to right.

nums = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 4
sorted windows: [-3,-1,1,3] [-3,-1,3,5] [-3,-1,3,5] [-3,3,5,6] [3,5,6,7]
element at position 1 of each: -1, -1, -1, 3, 5
result = [-1, -1, -1, 3, 5]
hints: Sorting every window costs O(n * k log k). Neighbouring windows differ by only one removed and one added element.
You need the r-th smallest element of a changing multiset, with r = (k - 1) / 2 + 1. Which structure supports insert, delete and rank queries?
Compress the values to ranks and use a Fenwick tree of counts. Add the new value, remove the old one, then find the r-th smallest by descending the tree.
editorial: Compress the distinct values of nums to ranks 1..m. A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) stores how many window elements have each rank. Inserting or deleting an element is one point update, O(log m).

To find the element of rank r = (k - 1) // 2 + 1, descend the tree from the highest power of two: at each step jump forward if the stored prefix count is still smaller than what remains to be found. This yields the smallest position whose prefix count reaches r in O(log m).

Total time is O(n log n) and space O(n). Two heaps with lazy deletion, or a sorted list with binary search, also work; the Fenwick approach has clean worst-case guarantees and handles duplicates naturally.
